samples.summary: The cross-tab write denial that enforces erase-on-sign-out is cleared by any `OfflineRuntime` mount carrying a stale cached identity
samples.evidence:
`rememberOfflineUser(userId)` unconditionally calls `permitOfflineWrites(userId)` (offline-erase.ts:77-82), which removes that account from the `wafflebase-offline-denied` localStorage list for EVERY tab. That deny list is, per its own doc comment (offline-erase.ts:121-143), "the feature's primary privacy control" on a shared device: it is what stops a still-mounted durable client from re-writing the document to the disk a sign-out just cleared (the SDK repairs a failed append by writing a fresh snapshot).

The attack/failure chain: user A signs out in tab A -> `eraseOfflineDataOnLogout` calls `denyOfflineWrites('A')` and erases, then clears the pending-erase marker on success. Tab B is still open on a document. `PrivateRoute` (PrivateRoute.tsx:15-30) uses `useQuery({queryKey:['me']})` gated on `isLoading`, so with the `['me']` entry still in the React Query cache it renders `me` truthy IMMEDIATELY while the background refetch (which will 401) is in flight. That renders `<OfflineRuntime userId={String(me.id)} />` (PrivateRoute.tsx:58), whose effect calls `rememberOfflineUser(userId)` on mount (offline-runtime.tsx:66) -> `permitOfflineWrites('A')`.

From that moment `isOfflineWritePermitted('A')` is true again in every tab, so `DurableYorkieProvider`'s store predicate `getOfflinePersistenceEnabled(userId) && isOfflineWritePermitted(userId)` (durable-yorkie-provider.tsx:185-187) permits writes, and A's document content is written back to the shared device's disk. Nothing re-erases it: the pending-erase marker was cleared on the successful erase, so only `collectStale`'s thirty-day sweep will ever remove it. A remount of `PrivateRoute` is reachable by navigating out to a public route (`/shared/:token`, `/t/:id`) and back, or by any route-tree remount before the 401 lands.

The denial should be lifted only by a fresh authenticated session (a `fetchMe` that actually resolved on this navigation), not by a mount that inherited a cached identity from the session that was just signed out.

samples.summary: `dropAllForUser` walks only the header index, so snapshot rows with no header survive a deliberate sign-out with document content on disk
samples.evidence:
`dropAllForUser` enumerates via `headerKeysWhere(BY_USER, IDBKeyRange.only(userId))` (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:1137) and purges only those keys; archives are handled separately by `dropArchivesWhere(BY_USER, ...)`. A snapshot row whose header is missing is named by neither.

The code itself states the consequence at wafflebase-doc-store.ts:1246-1249, inside `collectStale`: "anything with a snapshot but no header. Every other path here walks the header indexes, so such a row is unreachable by all of them while `load` still reports the document as present - a permanent quota leak holding document content that **logout cannot erase**." `orphanSnapshotKeys()` (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:1298) is reached only from `collectStale`, i.e. the thirty-day sweep.

So the design's stated promise - a deliberate sign-out leaves nothing of that account's document content on a shared device - has a gap: any orphan snapshot (a torn write, a future schema change, a rollback) keeps full gzip'd document bytes readable on the machine for up to thirty days after sign-out, and the erase reports success. `atomically()` makes orphans rare rather than impossible, which is why `collectStale` bothers to handle them at all. `eraseOfflineData`/`dropAllForUser` should run the same orphan sweep.

samples.summary: A deleted workspace is indistinguishable from a deleted document on a non-acting member's device, so their archive survives and recovery republishes the content into a workspace they own or share
samples.evidence:
The design's cleanup rule (`docs/design/offline-local-persistence.md`, Storage table) says "Workspace deleted, or membership removed | Drop those entries **and their archives**", and `api/workspaces.ts` `deleteWorkspace` implements it with `purgeOfflineDocuments(doomed, { dropArchives: true })`. But that runs only on the device of whoever performed the delete.

On any OTHER member's device the only signal is the session-start reconcile, whose `isRevoked` (offline-runtime.tsx:103-110) drops an archive on a `403` and on nothing else. A deleted workspace cascades the document rows away, so `GET /documents/:id` answers `404` (documents.controller.ts:170-172), not `403`. The archive is therefore KEPT.

`offerRecoverableWork` then reads the same `404` as "deleted upstream" (offline-runtime.tsx, the `err.status !== 404 -> continue` arm), keeps the fallbacks, and `resolveRecoveryDestination(undefined)` (offline-copy-recovery.ts) picks a workspace the user belongs to - preferring a sole-member one, but falling back to `workspaces[0]` with `shared: true` when there is none, and also falling into that branch whenever `fetchMe()` or `fetchWorkspace()` fails. One click then materializes the full content of the deleted workspace's document as a new document in a workspace the member shares with other people.

Net effect: deleting a workspace (the action an operator would take for a "remove all our data" request) cannot reach other members' local archives, and the feature actively offers to republish that content to a new audience. The offer does name the destination, which bounds the harm to informed consent, but the stated rule that content must not outlive the authority to read it is not enforced off the acting device.

samples.summary: `randomSecret()` falls back to `Math.random()` for the salt whose only purpose is to make the Yorkie client key unguessable
samples.evidence:
`randomSecret()` (durable-session.ts:244-257) uses `crypto.getRandomValues` when available and otherwise fills the 8 bytes from `Math.random()`. That value is the entire defence described at durable-session.ts:80-104: without it a workspace peer who knows `userId` (the sequential member id) and `docKey` (`sheet-<id>` from the URL) can derive another member's client key, and Yorkie authorizes `ActivateClient`/`DeactivateClient` on token validity alone - so they can take over or repeatedly tear down that member's per-document client.

`Math.random()` is not a CSPRNG and is seeded/predictable in every engine, so on the fallback path the salt is recoverable and the key becomes derivable again. The inline comment argues the branch is unreachable because "`navigator.locks` and `crypto` are both secure-context APIs" - but `crypto.getRandomValues` is available in insecure contexts in all current browsers (only `crypto.subtle` is secure-context-gated), so the premise is wrong even though the branch is in practice dead. A security-relevant secret should throw or refuse durability rather than degrade to `Math.random()`.

samples.summary: `dropArchive(id)` performs no owner check, unlike `loadArchive` and `listArchives`
samples.evidence:
`loadArchive` refuses an archive belonging to another account (`if (!row || row.userId !== this.userId) return undefined;`) and `listArchives` reads through `index(BY_USER).getAll(this.userId)`. `dropArchive` (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:1118-1123) deletes by raw auto-increment id with no such check.

It is not reachable cross-account today - its only caller, `recoverOfflineCopy`, takes an id that came from `listRecoverableWork(store)` -> `store.listArchives()`, which is scoped - and the impact is destruction rather than disclosure. But it is the one member of the archive API that does not enforce the ownership invariant the other two do, so a future caller that takes an id from anywhere else silently deletes another account's only copy of unsent work.

samples.summary: The path-traversal regression test was relaxed from "every request URL carries the encoded id" to "some request URL carries it"
samples.evidence:
The suite at url.test.ts:75 exists to pin that every browser API module interpolating a route-param id keeps it in one path segment. The old assertion ran `expect(pathname).toContain(encodeURIComponent(TRAVERSAL))` for EVERY request a call produced; the new one (url.test.ts:170-174) only requires `paths.some(...)`.

The relaxation is needed - `deleteWorkspace` now issues a companion `fetchDocuments()` with no id (workspaces.ts `documentIdsIn`) - and the per-URL `not.toContain('/auth/logout')` check is retained, which still catches the one payload in use (`TRAVERSAL = "../../auth/logout"`, url.test.ts:68) wherever it is interpolated raw. So I could not turn it into a bypass.

What it does lose is the positive per-request property: a module that interpolated an id raw into a second URL would now pass as long as that URL happens not to normalize onto `/auth/logout` - e.g. a payload that escapes the API prefix onto a different sensitive route. Narrowing the `some` to "every URL that is supposed to carry the id" (or asserting against the full URL set per call) would keep the original strength while accommodating the companion request.

verdict.reason: Every claimed element is present as described. `rememberOfflineUser` unconditionally calls `permitOfflineWrites(userId)` (offline-erase.ts:75-82), which deletes the id from the shared `wafflebase-offline-denied` localStorage list (offline-erase.ts:192-195), lifting the denial in every tab. `denyOfflineWrites` is written only by logout (offline-erase.ts:330; grep found no other caller), and the pending-erase marker is cleared on a successful erase (offline-erase.ts:338), so nothing re-denies. `OfflineRuntime`'s mount effect calls `rememberOfflineUser(userId)` (offline-runtime.tsx:66) with no proof of a freshly resolved session, and `PrivateRoute` renders it from a cached `['me']` entry because it gates only on `isLoading` and never on error/staleness (PrivateRoute.tsx:15-30, 58) under a default `QueryClient` (App.tsx:100, gcTime 5 min). The durable store re-reads the predicate at write time (durable-yorkie-provider.tsx:185-187), so writes resume and re-persist the erased document. No cross-tab sign-out propagation (no BroadcastChannel/storage listener for identity) prevents tab B from holding the stale identity. This is a shared-device privacy control being silently bypassed — sensitive data exposure, in the security lane, major.
